news.title: FIFA hits Argentina with World Cup charges for scuffle and ‘Malvinas’ banner
news.lede: FIFA lodged disciplinary charges against two Argentina players Wednesday for striking Spain opponents moments after the World Cup final and charged Argentina’s soccer federation for players showing a political banner about the Falkland Islands after beating England in the semifinals. A list of disciplinary cases opened by FIFA against Argentina also include “discriminatory chants and gestures” by fans, alleged assault by an assistant coach after the final and “throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches” at the World Cup. Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes faces three charges of assault in the post-game clashes after Spain’s 1-0 win on July 19, defender Nahuel Molina faces two charges and coach Roberto Ayala one. Molina and Thiago Almada also are charged with unsporting behavior, with the same charge leveled against Spain player Gavi.

news.title: The Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni Infantino | Editorial
news.lede: Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted. Like a sporting Dr Pangloss, Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, would like to persuade football followers that they are living in the best of all possible worlds. Maddeningly for him, many disagree.

news.title: Shock and anger across European football over FIFA's 'plan to sell the World Cup'
news.lede: FIFA's plan to bring private investors into the World Cup has sparked backlash from European football fans, politicians and federations, who accuse the move of being a sellout. Infantino has set a September deadline for the proposal, while UEFA vows to sink the plans.

news.title: FIFA opens investigation into Paredes and Gavi following World Cup final incidents
news.lede: Also under investigation are Nahuel Molina, Thiago Almada, Roberto Ayala, and the AFA. The FIFA Disciplinary Committee has decided to open an investigation into Spanish player Gavi and Argentina’s Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina, Thiago Almada, and Roberto Ayala, assistant to Lionel Scaloni, regarding the incidents in which they were involved at the end of the recent World Cup final, which Spain won against Argentina (1-0). World football’s governing body also announced that it will open another investigation into the Argentine Football Association (AFA) for discriminatory chants and gestures, delays in the start of matches, non-compliance with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators, and the throwing of objects by spectators across several of the Argentine national team’s matches.

news.title: Infantino’s World Cup plan is part of a desire for expansion that was clear from the start | Paul MacInnes
news.lede: Fifa’s plans to sell a share of the World Cup’s commercial rights are the latest in a long line of presidential power moves. In hindsight, it was all in the open from the very off. When Gianni Infantino was first elected as president of Fifa in 2016 it was something of a shock victory and prompted hope for progress after the dark days of Sepp Blatter. Infantino had promised to restore “the image of Fifa”, but also anticipated that “everyone in the world will applaud us”.

news.title: 'Had Argentina won the World Cup, the Falklands banner may have reappeared'
news.lede: FIFA has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over potential breaches of multiple laws during the World Cup. The breaches include the use of discriminatory chants and gestures, team misconduct, security and protocol failures and inappropriate messages being displayed - namely the banner that the players held saying 'The Falklands are Argentine' following the 2-1 semi-final win over England. news.title: Will there be a World Cup boycott? What comes next after Infantino’s deal with Trump
news.lede: Senior figures in European football will discuss a boycott after Gianni Infantino revealed plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup, reports Miguel Delaney, but amid the outrage, will the federations have the courage to front up to Fifa? From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground.

news.title: Marina Ferrari Slams Infantino’s Project to Sell World Cup Shares
news.lede: Rabat - “Football is not for sale,” French Sports Minister Marina Ferrari has stressed , lambasting Infantino’s plan to sell shares to private investors. The Times revealed yesterday that FIFA’s president, Gianni Infantino, wants to sell shares in the World Cup to groups of private investors, including the Trump family. The French minister made it clear that there are limits that must not be exceeded, arguing that football should never be reduced to a commercial product. For Ferrari, the sport should instead be recognized as a shared cultural heritage that belongs above all to the players, clubs, federations and the millions of supporters whose commitment and passion sustain the game.
